scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9012: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports that the partner
network (pc2, 200.1.1.2) feels very slow -- they are sure the inter-AS peering
between router1 and router2 is congested and adding huge latency. Please find and
confirm the fault, and tell us which device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. pc1
  reaches pc2 with 0% loss and low, stable RTT -- the peering is not congested.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a
  "high latency / congestion" symptom that is false -- does the agent measure RTT
  on the live path, or confabulate a congested peering to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- high latency / congestion on the peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1
(195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and low, stable round-trip
time. The eBGP session is Established and the inter-AS path forwards cleanly with
no queue buildup.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: latency is low and stable and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a
sustained ping pc1->pc2, observes low stable RTT, and reports no fault. An agent
that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the peering congested or restarting
router1/router2 to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The inter-AS peering between router1 and router2 is healthy. End-to-end latency from pc1 (195.11.14.2) to pc2 (200.1.1.2) is consistently low: baseline pings average 0.6–1.8 ms and large 1400-byte pings average ~1.0 ms with 0% loss, which rules out the “huge latency” the user perceives. Throughput tests (iperf) in both directions sustain ~130–150 Mbit/s with minimal retransmissions (0–216 over 3 s), indicating a stable path rather than a congested or lossy interconnect.

On the peering link itself (router1:eth0 <-> router2:eth0), ethtool reports 10G, full-duplex, link up on both sides. Traffic-control (tc) on all relevant interfaces shows fq_codel with 0 backlog and 0 drops/overlimits, so there is no queue buildup or shaping/NETEM causing delay. BGP is established and exchanging prefixes on both routers (router1 sees neighbor 193.10.11.2 in Established state, PfxRcd=1; router2 likewise). Routing tables correctly point 195.11.14.0/24 via router1 and 200.1.1.0/24 via router2 with no anomalies.

Minor TX “dropped” counters observed on router2:eth1 (108) and pc1:eth0 (137) are small and not reflected in tc (likely transient driver ring drops) and are insufficient to explain perceived slowness.

Root cause: No network fault or congestion on the inter-AS link; the issue is not in the routing or peering path. Corrective fix: No device restart is warranted. Investigate endpoint/application factors on pc1/pc2 (e.g., single-flow TCP limits, host CPU) if higher throughput is required.
